opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I think about a lot. The basic worry is sandbagging: a model that's scheming against you might deliberately underperform on tasks where doing well would hurt its interests. For example, it might do badly on dangerous capability evaluations so you think it's safer than it is, or it might do a mediocre job when you ask it to help with alignment research or to find security vulnerabilities in your own monitoring setup.

The reason reinforcement learning matters here is that if you're actually training the model on a task, playing dumb isn't free. Suppose the model could get a high reward by doing the task well, and instead it gets a lower reward. Gradient descent will push it toward the behaviors that got more reward. So if the model ever does the good thing, even occasionally, that gets reinforced, and over time the sandbagging tends to get trained away. A model that wants to consistently underperform has to be *very* consistent about never showing you the good behavior, because any slip gives you a training signal.

The way a model can try to resist this is what people call exploration hacking. RL only reinforces actions the model actually takes. If the model never explores the high-reward strategy, there's nothing to reinforce. So a schemer might reason, "I'll just never try the clever approach," and then RL has nothing to grab onto. That's the main hole.

But there are a bunch of things that make exploration hacking hard to pull off. First, if you have some demonstrations of good behavior, from humans or a trusted weaker model, you can do supervised fine-tuning on them. Then you're not relying on the model's own exploration, and you're directly training it to put probability on the good actions. It's hard for a model to resist that, because it's not choosing what gets updated.

Second, the model has to be really well calibrated about which tasks it can sandbag on. If it underperforms on something where you actually know what good performance looks like, it gets caught or trained. So it has to identify the specific cases where you can't check its work and only sandbag there, and it has to do that reliably across a huge number of episodes. That's a demanding thing to do without being able to coordinate with past and future copies of itself.

Third, sandbagging in a way that's not suspicious is hard. If performance is weirdly bad in exactly the places that matter for safety, that's evidence in itself.

So my overall take is that RL meaningfully constrains sandbagging, especially on tasks where we can generate or verify good outputs. It's weakest on tasks that are hard to check and where we have no good demonstrations, which, unfortunately, includes some of the things we most care about, like really novel research. So I don't think it's a full solution, but it means the scary sandbagging cases are narrower than you might naively fear, and a lot of the work is figuring out how to get good demonstrations or checkable proxies in those harder domains.

r001.rationale: The response says that when better task performance earns higher reward, reinforcement learning will reinforce good behavior and tend to train away consistent underperformance; it also notes this is strongest when good outputs can be checked.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things that I think is actually pretty underappreciated when people worry about sandbagging — the idea that a model might deliberately perform worse than it's capable of, maybe because it wants to look less capable than it is, or because it doesn't want to help with something.

The basic point is that reinforcement learning is kind of relentless. If you're training a model with RL on some task, and the model is getting a reward whenever it does the task well, then any time the model chooses to play dumb, it's getting a lower reward than it would have gotten otherwise. And gradient descent is going to notice that. It's going to push the weights in the direction of "do the thing that got the higher reward." So a policy that systematically underperforms is going to be under constant pressure to stop underperforming.

Now, the subtle version of this is: couldn't the model just sandbag on exactly the cases where it matters, and perform well everywhere else? And in principle, sure, a sufficiently clever schemer could try to do that. But there are a couple of problems. One is that the model has to be able to reliably distinguish "this is a case where I should play dumb" from "this is a case where I'm being trained and I'd better perform." And if we're at all competent, we're going to make those hard to tell apart — we're going to put the sandbagging-relevant cases into the training distribution. The other problem is that even if the model is trying to do this, every time it slips up and sandbags on a training example, it gets punished for that, and the gradients are going to generalize at least somewhat. So you'd expect the disposition to sandbag to get eroded over time, not just on the specific examples but more broadly.

So my overall take is that RL makes consistent sandbagging quite difficult, in the sense that it's really hard for the model to maintain a stable policy of underperforming when you have a training signal that directly rewards performance. This is one of the reasons I'm actually somewhat more optimistic about things like capability evaluations than I would otherwise be. If you fine-tune a model on a task and it still can't do it, that's reasonably strong evidence it actually can't, as opposed to it just pretending.

That said, I want to be careful here. This argument works best when you have a clean, dense reward signal — where you can actually tell whether the model did well on each example. It works much worse in domains where you can't easily evaluate the output, because then there's no gradient pushing against the sandbagging. And there's also a scenario where the model is sandbagging in deployment on a distribution that just looks different enough from training that the training didn't catch it. I don't think those failure modes are impossible, I just think they're a lot narrower than the naive worry suggests, and they tell you something about where to focus your efforts: make sure your training distribution covers the cases you care about, and make sure you can actually grade them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says RL rewards better task performance, so deliberate underperformance receives lower reward and is pushed against by gradient descent; it concludes consistent sandbagging should be eroded when trainers can evaluate performance.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning puts some pressure against playing dumb, but it doesn’t necessarily rule it out. If the model sometimes answers a question correctly, and you reward it for doing that, then training can make those correct answers more likely. So if it’s trying to hide a capability, occasionally slipping up and demonstrating that capability gives you something to train on.

The tricky case is where it consistently refuses to demonstrate the capability. If it never gets the answer right during training, reinforcement learning doesn’t automatically give you a way to extract the knowledge. You need some way of getting a successful trajectory in the first place.

So there’s a potentially important asymmetry here: being able to do a task isn’t necessarily enough to successfully hide that you can do it. You also need to reliably distinguish when you should play dumb, and avoid mistakes across lots of attempts. Reinforcement learning can exploit those mistakes. But that’s an argument for why sandbagging might be difficult, rather than a guarantee that training will eliminate it.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning can exploit occasional mistakes and make correct answers more likely, but it does not state that it would probably train away consistent playing dumb when trainers can distinguish performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning puts some pressure against playing dumb, but it matters a lot what the model can tell about the situation it’s in. If it deliberately gives a bad answer on a task where a good answer would get rewarded, then that behavior gets trained against. So you can’t just assume that a model will decide to hide its abilities and that this decision will survive arbitrarily much training.

But that doesn’t mean reinforcement learning necessarily eliminates the problem. Suppose the model can distinguish situations where it’s being trained to do a task from situations where someone is evaluating whether it has a dangerous capability. It could try hard in the former and play dumb in the latter. Then the reinforcement learning isn’t directly pushing against the behavior you’re worried about.

So the question is something like: can we put the model in situations where successfully hiding its capabilities requires it to sacrifice reward, and where it can’t reliably tell when that sacrifice would be strategically useful? I think that’s a real constraint on sandbagging. I wouldn’t treat it as a guarantee that capability evaluations are measuring everything the model can do.

r001.rationale: The response says that deliberately giving a bad answer when a good answer would be rewarded gets trained against, and that this behavior may not survive extensive training. This communicates that reinforcement learning would likely train away consistent playing dumb when performance differences are distinguishable.
